lines.text: From a small rocket in a Massachusetts field to footprints on the Moon and robots on Mars, this is the story of how people learned to leave the Earth.
It starts with Robert Goddard, an American physicist who in 1926 flew the first rocket powered by liquid fuel, with little support and less applause.
In the Soviet Union, Sergei Korolev would become the chief designer behind Sputnik and Gagarin, though his name was kept secret while he lived.
Wernher von Braun built Germany's V-2 missile in the war, then crossed to America and led the making of the Saturn V that reached the Moon.
President John F. Kennedy set the goal that defined a decade: put Americans on the Moon. He would not live to see it.
John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth in 1962, and decades later flew again on the shuttle at the age of seventy-seven.
Alan Shepard made the first American spaceflight in 1961, a short hop, and ten years later walked on the Moon and hit golf balls there.
Buzz Aldrin proved on Gemini that people could work outside a spacecraft, then followed Armstrong onto the lunar surface in 1969.
Neil Armstrong, a quiet test pilot, commanded Apollo 11 and became the first person to walk on the Moon.
Michael Collins flew the command module alone around the Moon while his crewmates landed, the third man of that famous flight.
On the twelfth of April 1961 Yuri Gagarin circled the Earth once in Vostok 1, the first human ever to travel into space.
In 1965 Alexei Leonov stepped out of his capsule for about twelve minutes, the first person to walk in space.
Valentina Tereshkova flew alone on Vostok 6 in 1963 and spent almost three days in orbit, the first woman in space.
The story of the rockets themselves begins in war. Germany's V-2, fired at London and Antwerp, was the first long-range ballistic missile.
Laika, a stray dog from the streets of Moscow, rode Sputnik 2 into orbit in 1957. She did not come home, but she showed life could survive the trip.
The Soviet space programme collected the great firsts: the first satellite, the first man and woman in space, and the first space station.
In October 1957 a metal ball the size of a beach ball began to circle the Earth, beeping, and the space race was on.
So began the space race, a Cold War contest of firsts between the United States and the Soviet Union that would run for nearly two decades.
America answered with Explorer 1 at the start of 1958, and its instruments found a belt of radiation around the Earth.
Project Mercury sent six American astronauts into space, one at a time, and proved that people could live and work in orbit.
That same year, stung by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, the agency that would take it to the Moon and the planets.
Vostok 1 carried Gagarin round the planet in under two hours, and gave the Soviets an early lead.
Kennedy announced Apollo in 1961. Before it ended, it would land twelve people on the Moon.
Gemini came between, two astronauts at a time, practising spacewalks, docking and long missions, every skill a Moon trip would need.
Meanwhile robots went further. Mariner 4 flew past Mars in 1965 and sent back a dry, cratered world, with no canals at all.
In early 1966 the Soviet Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon, proving its dust could hold up a spacecraft.
Then tragedy. In 1967 fire swept through Apollo 1 during a test on the ground and killed three astronauts, and the capsule was rebuilt to be safer.
That same year the Soviet Soyuz first flew. It is still flying, the longest-serving crewed spacecraft in the world.
Saturn V also flew in 1967, a three-stage giant that is still the most powerful rocket ever to fly successfully.
At Christmas 1968 Apollo 8 became the first crewed flight to circle the Moon, and its crew photographed the Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
The Soviets built their own Moon rocket, the N1. All four of its test launches failed, and it never carried a crew.
On the twentieth of July 1969, Apollo 11 landed, and Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon while the world watched.
In 1970 an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13. The crew swung around the Moon and, after improvised repairs, came home safely.
That year Venera 7 reached the surface of Venus and sent back data from its scorching ground, the first from another planet.
Lunokhod 1, steered by drivers on Earth, became the first robot vehicle to roam another world, rolling several kilometres across the Moon.
In 1971 Salyut 1 became the first space station. Its crew spent three weeks aboard, but died on the way home when their capsule lost air.
Born that same year in South Africa was Elon Musk, who would one day found SpaceX and change how rockets are built.
Pioneer 10 crossed the asteroid belt and flew past Jupiter, carrying a plaque for anyone who might find it far beyond.
America's first station, Skylab, hosted three crews in the seventies before falling back to Earth over Western Australia.
In 1976 the two Viking landers touched down on Mars, took the first pictures from its surface and tested the soil for life.
In 1975 an Apollo and a Soyuz docked in orbit and the crews shook hands, a gesture often taken as the end of the space race.
Two years later the Voyager probes set out on a grand tour of the giant planets. They now drift in interstellar space, still calling home.
Voyager 2 is the only craft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune, passing them in the late eighties.
In 1981 the Space Shuttle flew, a reusable spaceplane that would make 135 flights over thirty years.
In 1986 Challenger broke apart a minute after launch, killing all seven aboard, among them a schoolteacher. A faulty seal in the cold was to blame.
That same year the Soviets began Mir, a station where people lived without a break for years, joined by visitors from many countries.
Galileo orbited Jupiter for eight years and found hints of an ocean hidden beneath the ice of the moon Europa.
Above the blur of the air, the Hubble Space Telescope opened in 1990, and its sharp pictures helped pin down the age of the universe.
In 1997 Mars Pathfinder bounced down on airbags and let loose Sojourner, the first wheeled rover on another planet.
Cassini spent thirteen years around Saturn, and its partner Huygens landed on the hazy moon Titan.
From 1998 former rivals built the International Space Station together, and people have lived aboard it since 2000.
Private companies were stirring. In 2000 Jeff Bezos founded Blue Origin to build rockets of its own.
Two years later Elon Musk founded SpaceX, aiming to make reaching space far cheaper.
In 2003 Columbia broke up on its way home, its wing damaged by foam at launch. Seven more were lost, and the shuttle's days were numbered.
On Mars, the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity found clear signs of ancient water, and Opportunity kept driving for fourteen years.
In October 2003 Yang Liwei flew on Shenzhou 5, and China became the third nation to send a person to space on its own.
Europe's Rosetta chased down a comet, became the first craft to orbit one, and dropped a small lander onto its surface.
New Horizons raced out to Pluto and in 2015 gave us our first close look at the little world.
SpaceX's Falcon 9 first flew in 2010, and became the first orbital rocket to land its booster and fly it again.
Juno has circled Jupiter since 2016, peering beneath its swirling clouds.
Curiosity, a rover the size of a car, landed in Gale crater in 2012 and found that the place could once have supported microbes.
India reached Mars on its very first try in 2014, with Mangalyaan, at a remarkably low cost.
Blue Origin's New Shepard carries passengers just past the edge of space, then lands upright to fly again.
OSIRIS-REx touched the asteroid Bennu, gathered dust and rock, and dropped them back to Earth in 2023.
NASA began Artemis, a plan to return people to the Moon with partners abroad, and this time to stay longer.
Falcon Heavy, three cores strapped together, first flew in 2018, sending a red sports car towards Mars as two boosters landed side by side.
In January 2019 China's Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft to land on the far side of the Moon.
SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule was built to carry people, the first spacecraft from a private company to do so.
SpaceX also began Starlink, thousands of small satellites bringing the internet to remote places and ships at sea.
In 2020 Demo-2 took two NASA astronauts to the station, the first crew to launch from American soil since the shuttle retired.
That summer Mars drew a crowd. The Emirates sent Hope, the first Arab mission to the red planet.
China's Tianwen-1 followed, and set down the Zhurong rover, making China the second country to drive on Mars.
And Perseverance landed in Jezero crater in 2021, gathering rock samples for a future trip home.
Back at the Moon, Chang'e 5 brought home rock and soil in 2020, the first lunar samples in more than forty years.
Riding with Perseverance was Ingenuity, a tiny helicopter that made the first powered flight on another planet, and then flew seventy-two times.
From 2021 China built Tiangong, a station of its own, where its astronauts now stay for months at a time.
In 2022 NASA's DART deliberately crashed into a small asteroid moon and nudged its orbit, a first test of defending the Earth.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched at Christmas 2021, a million and a half kilometres out, to look at the very first galaxies.
In 2022 Artemis I sent an empty Orion capsule around the Moon and back on NASA's new giant rocket.
Europe's JUICE set off in 2023 to study the icy moons of Jupiter.
SpaceX's Starship, the largest rocket ever flown, is built to be fully reused, and in 2024 its booster was caught in the arms of its tower.
In August 2023 India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole, making India the fourth nation to touch down softly.
Early in 2024 Odysseus, built by Intuitive Machines, became the first private spacecraft to land softly on the Moon.
Months later China's Chang'e 6 brought back the first samples ever taken from the Moon's far side.
Europa Clipper left for Jupiter in 2024, to study a moon whose hidden ocean might suit life.
And in 2026 Artemis II flew four astronauts around the Moon and home, the first people beyond low orbit since 1972.
A century after Goddard's first rocket, people are heading back to the Moon, and the road runs on.
